sections.title: Why Custom Integration Matters
learningObjectives: Understand why REST API access exists beyond the standard ANT interface
Recognize which kinds of facilities and systems typically need custom integration
sections.content: Most MoRo deployments operate entirely through the ANT interface. But some facilities need MoRo's fleet behavior tied into systems ANT doesn't natively cover - a custom dashboard, a third-party WMS without a pre-built connector, or automated reporting into an existing facility system. MoRo's REST API exists for exactly this: programmatic access to fleet control and status beyond what the standard interface provides.

keyTerms.note: A standard way for external software to communicate with a system programmatically, used here to extend fleet control and data access beyond the ANT interface.
Software that tracks inventory and manages warehouse operations, often integrated with MoRo for triggering and reporting.

sections.title: What the API Exposes
learningObjectives: Understand the general categories of functionality available via the API
Recognize the distinction between read access and control access
sections.content: At a conceptual level, MoRo's API exposes two broad categories: read access (fleet status, mission history, unit health - pulling data out) and control access (assigning missions, triggering actions - pushing commands in). Specific endpoint documentation, authentication requirements, and rate limits are being finalized with DiFacto's engineering team and will be added to this module once confirmed.

keyTerms.note: A kind of API access for pulling data out, such as fleet status, mission history and unit health.
A kind of API access for sending commands in, such as assigning missions or triggering actions.
A specific address a program calls to request data or an action.

video.title: Read and control: the MoRo API in 30 seconds
video.transcript: The MoRo API, in 30 seconds. Read access pulls data out. Fleet status, mission history, unit health. Control access pushes commands in. It can assign missions and trigger actions. A request can move physical equipment. So only authorized systems should have control access.

sections.title: Authentication and Access Control
learningObjectives: Understand the general principle of API authentication
Recognize why access control matters for a system with physical-world control capability
sections.content: Because API control access means a request can move physical equipment, authentication and access control are not optional considerations - they're central to safe integration design. The specific authentication mechanism (API keys, tokens, or another method) will be detailed here once confirmed, but the underlying principle holds regardless of mechanism: only authorized systems should have control-level API access, and that access should be scoped as narrowly as the integration actually requires.

keyTerms.note: Proving that a system or user is who it claims to be before it is allowed access.

sections.title: Common Integration Patterns
learningObjectives: Understand typical use cases for custom API integration
Recognize when API integration is the right tool versus when it's unnecessary complexity
sections.content: Common patterns include pulling fleet status into a facility-wide dashboard, triggering missions automatically from an external system event (an order placed, a production run completed), or logging MoRo data into an existing analytics platform. Not every facility needs this - if ANT and standard integrations (such as the FANUC I/O handshake in L3B-M4) already meet operational needs, custom API work adds complexity without corresponding value. This module is for situations where a genuine integration gap exists.

sections.title: Testing an Integration Safely
learningObjectives: Understand the principle of testing API-triggered actions before production use
Recognize the elevated risk of control-access testing compared to read-access testing
sections.content: Testing an integration that only reads data carries little operational risk. Testing one with control access - the ability to trigger missions or actions - carries real risk if something behaves unexpectedly, since it can move physical equipment. Any control-access integration should be tested in a supervised, low-stakes setting first, the same principle covered for new missions generally in L2-M1, but with added caution given the integration layer sits further from direct human oversight.

sections.title: Maintaining an Integration Over Time
learningObjectives: Understand that an integration isn't a one-time build
Recognize ongoing responsibilities once an integration is live
sections.content: Once live, a custom integration needs monitoring the same way any production system does - watching for failed requests, unexpected behavior, or changes on either side (MoRo's API or the external system) that break assumptions the integration was built on. Treat an integration as something you maintain, not something you build once and forget.

questions.question: Why does MoRo's REST API exist alongside the ANT interface?
options: To allow programmatic integration with systems ANT doesn't natively cover
It's a redundant backup system that takes over whenever the ANT interface goes down
questions.feedback: Correct. The API extends integration capability beyond what the standard interface provides.

questions.question: Which of these is a control-access action?
questions.feedback: Correct. Control access sends commands in, such as assigning missions or triggering actions.

questions.question: An integration only pulls fleet status into a dashboard. What access should it have?
options: Read and control access, in case control is needed later
Read access only, scoped as narrowly as the integration requires
questions.feedback: Correct. Access should be scoped as narrowly as the integration actually requires.

questions.question: ANT and standard integrations already meet a facility's operational needs. What does custom API work add?
questions.feedback: Correct. If ANT and standard integrations already meet operational needs, custom API work adds complexity without corresponding value.

questions.question: How should a control-access integration be tested first?
options: The same way as a read-only integration
questions.feedback: Correct. Test any control-access integration in a supervised, low-stakes setting first. It can trigger real physical actions if something behaves unexpectedly.
